papers.title: Associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy procedure versus conventional two-stage hepatectomy for colorectal liver metastasis
papers.journal_full: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
papers.authors: Shiraiwa D, Riera R, Kleinubing D, Linhares M, Supported by the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Review Group
papers.abstract:
RATIONALE: Staged surgical procedures, such as two-stage hepatectomy and associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) technique, use the liver regenerative capacity to stimulate growth of the future liver remnant. These procedures can be used in people with extensive colorectal liver metastases when the future liver remnant is too small to allow a safe postoperative recovery after major hepatectomy. Compared with conventional two-stage hepatectomy, although ALPPS results in faster and larger growth of the future liver remnant, the evidence regarding its impact on major postoperative complications, perioperative mortality, recurrence rates, and long-term survival is conflicting.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of liver partition and portal vein ligation for a staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) procedure versus conventional two-stage hepatectomy in people with colorectal liver metastases.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials in the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Embase, three other databases, online trial registries, grey literature databases, and reference lists of identified studies; we also retrieved additional information from the included trial authors. Our last study search was on 4 December 2025.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Randomised clinical trials comparing ALPPS versus conventional two-stage hepatectomy in adults with colorectal liver metastases who were unable to undergo complete resection because the future liver remnant was estimated to be < 30% of the total liver volume.
OUTCOMES: The critical outcomes were perioperative all-cause mortality at 90 days, all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Other important outcomes included overall survival, disease-free survival, and resection rate. For our primary analysis, we used data at the maximum follow-up, except for perioperative mortality, analysed at 90 days after operation.
RISK OF BIAS: We used the Risk of Bias 2.0 (RoB 2) tool.
SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used standard Cochrane methodological procedures to develop the review. We did not perform meta-analysis because only one trial met the inclusion criteria. We expressed dichotomous outcomes as risk ratios (RR), continuous outcomes as mean differences (MD), and time-to-event outcomes as hazard ratios (HR), all with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), using RevMan. We used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of the evidence.
INCLUDED STUDIES: The included trial was a six-centre, publicly funded, Scandinavian randomised clinical trial. The trial investigators randomised 100 participants (mean age: 65 ± 10 years; male-to-female ratio: 2.34:1.0). After randomisation, two participants in the ALPPS (1 severe comorbidity; 1 total liver volume > 30%) and one participant in the two-stage hepatectomy group (progressive disease) could not proceed to the intervention and were excluded. One other participant was lost to follow-up after emigrating. The trial was described in 15 publications. The trial provided data for all outcomes of our review. We followed the analytical approach reported by the trial authors, using a modified intention-to-treat population where applicable and available data otherwise.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: The evidence suggests that ALPPS, compared with two-stage hepatectomy, results in little to no difference in perioperative all-cause mortality at 90 days (RR 1.36, 95% CI 0.32 to 5.76; I2 not applicable; 1 study; 97 participants; low-certainty evidence) and probably results in little to no difference in all-cause mortality at maximum follow-up (93 months) (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.03; 1 study, 97 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The trial reported a mean quality-adjusted survival MD of 1.25 quality-adjusted life years (QALY) (95% CI 1.08 to 1.42) for participants randomised to ALPPS, and MD 1.11 QALY (95% CI 0.94 to 1.27) for participants randomised to two-stage hepatectomy, with an estimated MD between the groups of 0.14 QALY (95% CI -0.32 to 0.60). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of ALPPS, compared with two-stage hepatectomy, on health-related quality of life (MD 0.14, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.54; 1 study, 97 participants; very low-certainty evidence) (maximal follow-up: two years) and on the rate of serious adverse events (maximal follow-up: 30 days) (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.74; 1 study, 72 participants; very low-certainty evidence). ALPPS probably results in little to no difference in the overall survival of people with colorectal liver metastases (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.24; 1 study, 97 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) (median 93 months) and results in little to no difference in disease-free survival (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.40; 1 study, 97 participants; low-certainty evidence) (median 93 months), but probably results in a large increase in resection rates (RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.07; 1 study, 97 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) (maximum follow-up: eight weeks), compared with two-stage hepatectomy. We downgraded the certainty of evidence for risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence derives from data from only one randomised clinical trial, with a low number of participants and events. We are very uncertain about the effect of ALPPS on health-related quality of life and the rate of serious adverse events (30 days of follow-up) compared with two-stage hepatectomy. We are uncertain whether there is little to no difference between ALPPS and two-stage hepatectomy in perioperative mortality at 90 days after operation and in disease-free survival. ALPPS, compared with two-stage hepatectomy, probably results in little to no difference in all-cause mortality at maximum follow-up (93 months) and in overall survival of people with colorectal liver metastases (median 93 months), but probably results in a large increase in resection rates (eight-week follow-up). The certainty of the evidence for the presented outcomes was very low, low, or moderate. We lack randomised trials comparing these two strategies to identify the best approach for routine use in surgical practice. Evidence from low- and middle-income countries is lacking. The choice of ALPPS should carefully consider clinical characteristics of the patients. More high-quality trials with large numbers of participants are needed to provide information on the risks and benefits of ALPPS for people with colorectal liver metastases.
FUNDING: This review does not have dedicated funding.
REGISTRATION: Protocol: published 08 March 2022, available in the Cochrane Library at https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD014608.

papers.title: Immunonutrition vs. Standard Oral Nutritional Supplements in Prehabilitation for Colorectal Cancer Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial Assessing Morbidity and Body Composition by Computed Tomography
papers.authors: Ugalde B, Juez L, Ruiz-Torres I, Perea-Fuentes I, Martos S, DeVicente I
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Perioperative immunonutrition (IMN) has been proposed to improve outcomes after colorectal surgery. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, and few studies have assessed morbidity together with computed tomography (CT)-derived body composition. We compared IMN with standard oral nutritional supplementation (SONS) in patients undergoing colorectal cancer surgery, evaluating postoperative complications and changes in body composition. Methods: Two-arm open-label randomized clinical trial including sixty patients (SONS: n = 30; IMN: n = 30). Postoperative complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification, and the Comprehensive Complication Index (CCI). Body composition was quantified using pre- and postoperative CT scans, analyzing the skeletal muscle mass index (SMMI) and psoas area. Results: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups, except for a higher age in the IMN group (p = 0.036). Overall morbidity was 40% in SONS and 50% in IMN (95%CI: -0.35 to 0.15). No differences were observed in the CCI (14.8 ± 23.1 vs. 15.7 ± 19.0, 95%CI: -11.8 to 10.0). Very major morbidity (Clavien ≥ IIIb) was comparable between groups (p = 0.687). At follow-up there was a decline in handgrip strength in SONS whereas it remained stable in IMN (p = 0.030 for the interaction). Also, there was a decrease in SMMI (-2.33, 95%CI: -1.19 to -3.48 cm2/m2) and psoas area (-1.15, 95%CI: -0.67 to -1.65 cm2) in SONS, whereas in IMN they remained stable: SMMI (-1.48, 95%CI: 1.04 to -3.99 cm2/m2), psoas area (-0.71, 95%CI: 0.36 to 1.78 cm2). Conclusions: IMN did not reduce morbidity compared with SONS when used as prehabilitation for colorectal cancer surgery. Exploratory findings suggested a possible attenuation of postoperative muscle loss with IMN.

papers.title: Dietary Polyphenols as Adjunctive Therapy for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
papers.authors: Dong Y, Xu H, Zhang D, Ren X, Wu X, Zheng Z
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dietary polyphenols have been studied as adjunctive therapies for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but trials vary in formulation, clinical setting, and outcome definitions. We evaluated efficacy and safety separately for ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD).
METHODS: We searched MEDLINE/PubMed, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov through 20 August 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2). Meta-analyses used MDs, SMDs, or ORs with 95% CIs. Quantitative synthesis was undertaken when studies were sufficiently comparable in clinical setting, outcome definition, and data structure; otherwise, results were summarized using study-level estimates. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261451126).
RESULTS: Twenty-one reports representing 19 randomized trials and 1048 participants were included. In conventional UC, polyphenols were associated with lower SCCAI scores (MD -1.32, 95% CI -1.81 to -0.83; I2 = 0%), whereas CRP/hs-CRP did not show a clear pooled effect (SMD 0.29, 95% CI -0.32 to 0.90; I2 = 83.7%). IBDQ-9 improved (MD 5.57, 95% CI 2.88 to 8.26). Clinical response favored supplementation (OR 4.90, 95% CI 3.04 to 7.89), as did induction of clinical remission (OR 5.98, 95% CI 3.08 to 11.59; I2 = 22.6%). Supplementation also favored endoscopic remission (OR 10.81, 95% CI 1.67 to 69.93; I2 = 69.4%), but the estimate was imprecise and sensitive to study-level risk of bias. In CD, the two randomized trials were not pooled due to targeting different clinical settings. Safety reporting was heterogeneous and sparse, with no consistent pattern of increased harm across trials.
CONCLUSIONS: Curcumin has the most extensive adjunctive evidence base in UC but effect estimates for several outcomes were imprecise or sensitive to study design. Evidence in CD is still lacking.

papers.title: Three-week ileostomy closure after colorectal surgery: a multicenter randomized trial of technical and postoperative outcomes
papers.authors: Debakey Y, Mostafa M, Kilany A, Madkour A, Mohamed A, El-Mikkawy A
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The optimal timing of temporary ileostomy closure following restorative colorectal surgery remains controversial. Although previous randomized studies have demonstrated the feasibility of early closure in carefully selected patients, the influence of closure timing on operative complexity has not been prospectively evaluated. This multicenter randomized controlled trial compared a standardized 3-week ileostomy closure strategy with conventional delayed closure, with particular emphasis on technical and postoperative outcomes.
METHODS: In this prospective multicenter randomized controlled trial, 224 patients undergoing restorative colorectal resection with temporary diverting ileostomy were randomized to either early ileostomy closure at 3 weeks (n = 112) or conventional delayed closure (n = 112). Eligibility for reversal required rigorous confirmation of anastomotic healing using standardized clinical and endoscopic assessment, with selective computed tomography using rectal contrast when clinically indicated. The primary outcome was operative complexity, evaluated using operative duration, intraoperative adhesion severity, and the requirement for extended adhesiolysis. Secondary outcomes included postoperative morbidity, Clavien-Dindo complication grade, length of hospital stay, readmission, reoperation, re-diversion, and delay in adjuvant chemotherapy.
RESULTS: Baseline demographic, clinical, and operative characteristics were comparable between the study groups. Early ileostomy closure was associated with significantly shorter operative duration (90 ± 12 vs. 130 ± 18 min; P < 0.001), substantially lower intraoperative adhesion severity (P = 0.04), and a markedly reduced requirement for extended adhesiolysis (5.4% vs. 21.4%; P < 0.001). Overall postoperative morbidity, Clavien-Dindo grade distribution, postoperative length of stay, readmission, reoperation, and mortality were comparable between groups. Delays in adjuvant chemotherapy occurred only in the early-closure group (3.6%), were limited to 1-4 weeks, and all affected patients subsequently commenced the planned oncologic treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: In carefully selected patients with confirmed anastomotic healing, 3-week ileostomy closure is a technically feasible and safe strategy following restorative colorectal surgery. Compared with conventional delayed closure, reversal at 3 weeks significantly reduced operative complexity without compromising short-term postoperative outcomes. These findings support selective implementation of a standardized 3-week ileostomy closure strategy and identify operative complexity as a key determinant when selecting the optimal timing of ileostomy reversal.
GOV IDENTIFIER: NCT05192018.

papers.title: Effect of Danggui Buxue Medicinal Diet on cancer-related fatigue in anemic colon cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy: A randomized controlled trial (CONSORT-compliant)
papers.authors: Wang L, Yang L, Wang L, Liang X, Wang Y, Huang B
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer-related fatigue (CRF) is one of the most common and distressing symptoms experienced by patients undergoing chemotherapy, and no gold standard for the treatment of CRF has been established. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of the Danggui Buxue Medicinal Diet on CRF in patients with chemotherapy-induced anemia following colon cancer surgery.
METHODS: A total of 96 patients admitted to the intestinal surgery ward and daytime chemotherapy ward of a tertiary hospital from May 2021 to December 2022 who met the inclusion criteria were selected and randomly divided into 2 groups: 48 patients in the control group and 48 in the experimental group. The control group received standard treatment and nursing care for postoperative chemotherapy for colon cancer, while the experimental group followed the control group's regimen and additionally received the Danggui Buxue Medicinal Diet for 21 consecutive days. Fatigue levels, blood counts, and inflammatory factors were compared before and after the intervention in both groups.
RESULTS: A total of 86 patients completed the study. After the intervention, the CRF scores in the experimental group were significantly lower than those in the control group (29.14 ± 2.58 vs 44.02 ± 4.25), with a between-group mean difference of -14.88 (95% confidence interval [CI], -16.38 to -13.38; P < .001). Hemoglobin levels were significantly higher in the experimental group than in the control group (115.26 ± 11.72 vs 106.52 ± 12.93), with a mean difference of 8.74 (95% CI, 3.45-14.03; P < .001). Red blood cell counts were also higher in the experimental group (mean difference 0.61; 95% CI, 0.44-0.78; P < .001). In addition, levels of inflammatory factors were significantly reduced, with interleukin-6 showing a mean difference of -16.28 (95% CI, -20.10 to -12.46; P < .001) and tumor necrosis factor-α showing a mean difference of -26.09 (95% CI, -29.80 to -22.38; P < .001).
CONCLUSION: The Danggui Buxue Medicinal Diet was associated with improvements in CRF, hematological parameters, and inflammatory markers in patients with chemotherapy-induced anemia following colon cancer surgery. These findings suggest that it may have potential as a supportive nutritional intervention for managing CRF in this population.

papers.title: Yield and efficiency of fecal immunochemical tests (FITs) for advanced colorectal neoplasia alone vs. with risk factors or risk prediction models: a descriptive systematic review
papers.authors: Imperiale T, Godfrey M, Thomas M, Sheel V, Hinrichs R
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Using the fecal immunochemical test (FIT) with risk factors for advanced colorectal neoplasia (AN - the combination of colorectal cancer and advanced precancerous polyps) could improve the yield of colonoscopy in both screening and diagnostic settings. In this systematic review, we evaluated: (1) yield and efficiency of FIT alone vs. FIT plus risk factors for screening and among FIT positive individuals; (2) study quality for these two settings.
METHODS: Following literature searches of Ovid MEDLINE and Embase from January 2010 to March 2026, two reviewers independently identified published English-language studies that evaluated FIT performance with and without risk factors among average-risk adults aged ≥ 40 years undergoing screening colonoscopy and among FIT positive subjects, independently extracted descriptive and numerical data, and evaluated study quality. We compared colonoscopy yield and efficiency of FIT alone versus FIT with risk prediction models and risk factors in screening and diagnostic studies.
RESULTS: From 1891 articles, we identified 9 screening studies and 10 diagnostic studies for a positive FIT. Both groups of studies were homogeneous in design and of good quality. In the nine screening studies, age, sex, BMI, family history of CRC, and smoking were most often used with varying model metrics and varying degrees of discrimination, and with modest-to-moderate improvements in efficiency at the cost of missing a proportion of AN. Among the ten diagnostic studies, the combination of fecal hemoglobin, age, sex, and smoking had the greatest improvement on yield and efficiency, but also missed a small proportion of AN.
CONCLUSIONS: In the screening setting, the yield of colonoscopy for AN improves when risk factors are used to stratify who is first screened with FIT vs. colonoscopy. In the diagnostic setting, risk factors help prioritize FIT-positive patients for diagnostic colonoscopy because of high risk for AN.

papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of VE1 Immunohistochemistry for BRAF p.V600E in Colorectal Carcinoma: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Șușu O, Botoncea M, Serac G, Beleaua M, Sipos T, Tăurean O
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: BRAF p.V600E status has diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic relevance in colorectal carcinoma. Molecular assays remain the reference methods, whereas mutation-specific BRAF (VE1 clone) immunohistochemistry offers a rapid tissue-based alternative. We evaluated VE1-molecular concordance and factors affecting diagnostic performance. Materials and Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched in August 2025 and updated on 27 July 2026 for English-language original studies published from 2014 through the update date. Eligible reports applied VE1 and a recognized molecular reference method to the same colorectal carcinoma specimens or a defined overlapping cohort. Study selection and data extraction were performed by one reviewer and independently verified by a second reviewer. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed at the estimate level with QUADAS-3. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, no meta-analysis was performed, and the findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: Of 704 database records, 358 unique records were screened; 38 full-text reports were assessed and 28 were included. Twenty-three reports or defined subcohorts provided complete or clearly reconstructible 2 × 2 comparisons. Sensitivity ranged from 74.6% to 100% and specificity from 66.7% to 100%. Most optimized protocols exceeded 90% for both measures, whereas selected sampling, weak or focal staining, post hoc thresholds, protocol effects, and selective molecular verification reduced reliability. Conclusions: VE1 immunohistochemistry may provide a rapid, locally validated triage method for detecting BRAF p.V600E in colorectal carcinoma. However, substantial heterogeneity and recurrent risk-of-bias concerns limit the generalizability of the available estimates and do not support universal substitution for molecular testing. Equivocal, technically inadequate, or clinically discordant results require molecular clarification.

papers.title: Comparative efficacy of common adjuvant treatments after resection of colorectal liver metastases: A systematic review and network meta-analysis
papers.authors: Zhou Y, Wang Q, Liu L, Wang X, Xue M, Xu J
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although adjuvant strategies such as systemic chemotherapy, regional nonsystemic chemotherapy, and ablation have been applied, the optimal adjuvant therapeutic strategy for resectable colorectal liver metastases remains uncertain in terms of overall survival and disease-free survival. This network meta-analysis aimed to determine the optimal adjuvant therapeutic strategy for patients with colorectal liver metastases.
METHODS: We searched potentially eligible studies in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure databases until July 2026. Pooled disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using R software.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies including 18 reports were included. For the DFS, except for adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (CT, HAIC) concomitant with intravenous CT, adjuvant CT and perioperative CT significantly improved DFS compared with surgery and adjuvant HAIC. There was no statistical difference between all therapeutic strategies for OS. Adjuvant HAIC concomitant with intravenous CT had the highest probability of being the best treatment for improving DFS (85.01%), followed by perioperative CT (11.75%) and adjuvant CT (3.17%); however, adjuvant HAIC concomitant with intravenous CT had the highest probability of being the best adjuvant treatment for improving OS (52.46%), followed by perioperative CT (40.25%) and adjuvant HAIC (5.25%).
CONCLUSION: Adjuvant CT may be the best for improving DFS, but perioperative CT may be the best for improving OS. However, the results should be validated further.

papers.title: Hepatic steatosis in inflammatory bowel disease: practical questions and evidence-based answers
papers.authors: Gisbert J, Lucendo A, Chaparro M
papers.abstract: Hepatic steatosis is among the most frequent hepatobiliary abnormalities in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but its clinical interpretation is increasingly complex. This narrative review provides evidence-based guidance for gastroenterologists managing adults with IBD and hepatic steatosis. Cohort and meta-analytic evidence indicates that hepatic steatosis affects approximately one-quarter to one-third of patients with IBD, although estimates vary according to diagnostic method, population selection, disease phenotype, metabolic burden, and study design. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) provides a useful framework for patients with cardiometabolic dysfunction, but a steatosis-centered approach is more inclusive in IBD because it accommodates lean or undernourished patients, inflammation-associated phenotypes, ileal or bile acid-related mechanisms, alcohol overlap, medication-related vulnerability, and mixed presentations. The main clinical priority is not merely to detect liver fat, but to identify meaningful fibrosis, cardiometabolic risk, and modifiable contributors. Normal aminotransferases do not exclude steatosis or fibrosis. Screening should be risk-based rather than universal. Fibrosis-4 index can be used pragmatically for initial triage in stable adults, but its IBD-specific limitations require cautious interpretation; transient elastography is most useful as a secondary fibrosis assessment or as a combined first test when readily available. Follow-up should be driven by fibrosis and cardiometabolic risk rather than by IBD alone, and hepatology referral should be reserved for elevated liver stiffness, persistent or cholestatic liver-test abnormalities, portal-hypertension features, suspected alternative liver disease, discordant tests, or clinically significant hepatic dysfunction. Hepatic steatosis alone should not determine IBD drug selection, although liver dysfunction and treatment-specific hepatotoxicity may modify monitoring or therapeutic choices.

papers.title: Microbiota-Associated Metabolites as Biomarkers and Therapeutic Opportunities in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.authors: Krysa K, Musz P, Ryś G, Serafin P, Wachowiak D, Jarmakiewicz-Czaja S
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel diseases, such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, are chronic inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract characterized by periods of active disease and remission. Their pathogenesis is multifactorial and involves genetic predisposition, immune response, environmental factors, and alterations in gut microbiota composition and function. Growing evidence suggests that gut microbiota-associated metabolites not only reflect disease activity but also participate in regulating the immune response and maintaining the integrity of the intestinal barrier. The most important groups of metabolites associated with inflammatory bowel diseases include short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives. Reduced fecal butyrate and acetate concentrations have been reported in inflammatory bowel diseases, although the diagnostic value of fecal short-chain fatty acids remains uncertain. Potential therapeutic approaches include short-chain fatty acid supplementation, particularly sodium butyrate, and dietary interventions aimed at increasing short-chain fatty acid concentrations; however, the clinical efficacy of short-chain fatty acid supplementation remains inconclusive, and evidence for dietary interventions is limited. In the future, the use of gut microbiota metabolites may be based on personalized strategies grounded in multiomic data, enabling precise modulation of the microbiota-metabolite-immune system axis.

papers.title: Modulation of Toll-like receptor signaling by intestinal bacteria in colorectal cancer
papers.journal_full: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
papers.authors: Wang S, Chen D, Yang D, Gao L, Zhang Y
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota contributes to intestinal homeostasis through dynamic interactions with epithelial, immune and stromal cells. Disruption of the balance, often termed dysbiosis, has been associated with colorectal cancer (CRC). At the same time, selected commensal bacteria have shown protective effects. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) provide an important molecular interface through which host cells detect bacterial components and initiate cellular responses. This Mini Review examines current evidence that intestinal bacteria and their products modulate TLR signaling in CRC, with effects that may promote or restrain tumor development. The reported mechanisms involve CRC cells as well as immune and stromal compartments within the tumor microenvironment. The available evidence does not support assigning a fixed biological effect to a bacterial species or TLR. Instead, the reported outcomes appear to vary with the nature of the bacterial stimulus, the responding cell and the disease setting. Resolving this context dependence may clarify how host cells translate bacterial stimuli through TLRs into responses that influence CRC progression and treatment response.

papers.title: Pitfalls and Complications During Common Anorectal Procedures
papers.journal_full: The Surgical clinics of North America
papers.authors: Brown J, Okonkwo A, Gagliano R, Clark C
papers.abstract: Nonoperative hemorrhoid procedures are generally less painful and complicated than operative ones, though surgery is sometimes necessary. Surgeons must understand the risks and complications of all procedures. Most acute anal fissures heal with nonoperative therapy, but surgery is sometimes needed. Lateral internal sphincterotomy offers the highest healing rate but risks continence changes, so sphincter-sparing options should be considered for high-risk patients. Anal abscess management (incision and drainage ± fistula procedure) risks defecatory dysfunction if the cause, location, and complexity are ignored.
